title: A.A.R.M.

jokes.text: The cold open spy-code exchange: 'The tea in Nepal is very hot.' / 'But the coffee in Peru is much hotter.'
jokes.setup: The episode opens with an unexplained, melodramatic spy-code exchange — someone emails secret daily codes to the office
jokes.punchline: The reveal that this elaborate KGB-style security protocol is protecting a paper company in Scranton, Pennsylvania
jokes.explanation: Classic Dwight cold open energy — his grandiose self-importance applied to a completely mundane context (paper security) is perfectly calibrated character comedy. The spy-thriller framing is committed and specific. Strong character integration because only Dwight would genuinely treat Dunder Mifflin like a state secret.

jokes.text: Dwight's confessional: 'I got these doors from a jewelry store that had recently gone out of business. Now they're protecting America's real treasure — Paper!'
jokes.setup: Dwight explains his security upgrade with genuine pride
jokes.punchline: 'America's real treasure — Paper!' delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: The line 'America's real treasure — Paper!' is a genuinely funny piece of Dwight-logic delivered with his characteristic earnestness. The detail that the jewelry store went out of business is a nice throwaway that adds texture. Strong economy — no wasted words.

jokes.text: Dwight confessional: 'Something that's been really missing from my life has been writing secret codes. It's not the KGB, but it's a start.'
jokes.setup: Dwight explains why he emails daily security codes
jokes.punchline: 'It's not the KGB, but it's a start' — treating paper-company security as a stepping stone to actual espionage
jokes.explanation: A concise, beautifully structured Dwight line. The aspiration ('not the KGB') combined with the patient realism ('but it's a start') reveals his entire psychology in eight words. This is the kind of economy that makes Dwight jokes feel effortless. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: The failed code exchange at the door — multiple wrong answers, getting 'warmer/colder' feedback like a children's game, culminating in Dwight threatening 'the steam'
jokes.setup: Someone (Jim) attempts to enter through Dwight's new secure doors using the daily code; gets it repeatedly wrong
jokes.punchline: The punishment for getting the code wrong three times is 'the steam' — harmless steam deployed to panic intruders — and the person eventually just submits to it
jokes.explanation: This sequence escalates beautifully: wrong codes → 'colder' feedback (treating it like a children's game) → the reveal of 'the steam' as a security measure → the victim resignedly saying 'give me the steam.' Each beat tops the last. 'I'd like to get harmful steam, but the prices are absurd' is a standout line that could anchor the whole bit. The resigned acceptance of the steam by the victim is the perfect button.

jokes.text: 'It's just harmless steam to panic intruders. I'd like to get harmful steam, but the prices are absurd!'
jokes.setup: Dwight explains the steam security system
jokes.punchline: He'd prefer 'harmful steam' but it's too expensive — a bureaucratic obstacle to his vision of genuine harm
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) the distinction between 'harmless' and 'harmful' steam as if it's a standard product category, (2) his genuine frustration that cost is the only barrier to deploying a weapon on coworkers, (3) the corporate-complaint framing ('the prices are absurd') applied to a monstrous desire. It's deeply Dwight-specific, perfectly economical, and wildly quotable. Approaches the calibration anchor for 8+ jokes.

jokes.text: The crowd outside chanting 'Break protocol! Break protocol! Break protocol!' while someone is being steamed
jokes.setup: The steam has been deployed as punishment for the code violation
jokes.punchline: Coworkers chanting 'break protocol' as if at a sporting event — the stakes of office security theater treated with crowd hysteria
jokes.explanation: A solid crowd-reaction button to the steam sequence. The chanting treats bureaucratic procedure like a stadium event, which is funny. Slightly weaker because the joke is mostly carried by the previous setup rather than standing on its own.

jokes.text: 'Oh, I'm saving a fortune on dry-cleaning.' — reaction after being steamed
jokes.setup: Someone has just been blasted with steam as a security measure
jokes.punchline: Finding the silver lining — the steam is an unexpected dry-cleaning substitute
jokes.explanation: Jim's signature deadpan response to absurdity — rather than objecting to being steamed, he finds a practical upside. Perfectly in character, great economy, and serves as an ideal button on the entire cold-open sequence.

jokes.text: Oscar's confessional: 'Ironic that now it's Angela who's living in the closet.'
jokes.setup: Oscar explains that Angela (whose husband the Senator was gay) got kicked out of her apartment after the divorce, and Oscar invited her to move in
jokes.punchline: 'Ironic that now it's Angela who's living in the closet' — a double meaning (literally in a small space, metaphorically reversing the gay-closet dynamic with the Senator)
jokes.explanation: An exceptional joke that rewards season-long investment. The setup (Angela's senator husband was in the closet, she didn't know) pays off in a line that is (1) perfectly economical, (2) genuinely witty wordplay, (3) delivered by the one character for whom the joke has maximum resonance. Oscar's knowing delivery makes it land harder. This is the kind of character-integrated wordplay that elevates sitcom writing — comparable to the 8.0 calibration anchor.

jokes.text: Angela threatening to call child protective services over saddle shoes with denim
jokes.setup: Angela is living in Oscar's closet at his charity, critiquing his fashion choices for her son
jokes.punchline: 'Saddle shoes with denim? I will literally call child protective services.' — treating a minor fashion faux pas as grounds for involving the state
jokes.explanation: Angela's rigid moralism weaponized toward genuinely trivial things is her defining comic trait. Using child protective services as the enforcement mechanism for a clothing disagreement is a perfectly calibrated escalation. Strong character integration — only Angela would make this threat.

jokes.text: Oscar sends Phillip off with 'Go get 'em, honey.' Angela responds 'Oh, don't worry. They'll get got.'
jokes.setup: Oscar gives a warm send-off to Angela and the baby
jokes.punchline: Angela's response 'They'll get got' is menacing and bizarre — a weirdly tough-guy response from a prim woman sending a baby to daycare
jokes.explanation: A small but effective character joke. 'They'll get got' is an unexpectedly street-tough phrase from Angela, playing on her hidden ferocity beneath the prim exterior. Brief and punchy.

jokes.text: Dwight's confessional listing his achievements: 'Manager of Dunder Mifflin. Check! Owner of a 1,600-acre beet farm. Check! Engaged to be married to an actual milkmaid. Check... on that later today.'
jokes.setup: Dwight tallies his life accomplishments with the satisfaction of a man who has conquered everything
jokes.punchline: 'Check... on that later today' — he hasn't actually done the last one yet, revealed mid-list with no change in delivery
jokes.explanation: The rhythm of the confessional (check, check, check... oh wait) is nicely constructed. 'An actual milkmaid' as a life goal is wonderfully Dwight-specific. The stumble into 'on that later today' is a good structural subversion of the established pattern.

jokes.text: 'It was made from a bullet I took out of her left buttock. She was a moonshiner shot by Adolph Coors. This is my grandmother's buttock bullet ring.'
jokes.setup: Dwight shows his grandmother's engagement ring with apparent tenderness
jokes.punchline: The ring was made from a bullet removed from his grandmother's buttock — she was a moonshiner shot by Adolph Coors — ending with the formal title 'my grandmother's buttock bullet ring'
jokes.explanation: A masterpiece of Dwight absurdism. Each clause escalates: grandmother's ring → bullet → from her buttock → shot by Adolph Coors (name-drop that lands because it's weirdly specific and historically plausible) → the formal christening 'my grandmother's buttock bullet ring.' The specificity of 'left buttock' and 'Adolph Coors' make it feel real in the Dunder Mifflin universe. The callback later in the proposal scene earns additional points. This is legitimately exceptional writing — approaches the calibration anchor for 9+ material.

jokes.text: Andy introducing himself to the audition line: 'Name is Andrew Bernard. You might know me from a TV documentary that's premiering tonight.'
jokes.setup: Andy is in line to audition for a singing competition show
jokes.punchline: He name-drops the documentary as a credential, as if being a background employee on a workplace doc is celebrity currency
jokes.explanation: A nice piece of character comedy — Andy's self-delusion about his fame is consistent with his season 9 arc. The meta-reference to the documentary airing tonight is a good layered joke for viewers. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: 'Also killed it in local theater, and I am fresh off of a hot industrial flick.'
jokes.setup: Andy continues listing his credentials to strangers in line
jokes.punchline: 'A hot industrial flick' — corporate training videos positioned as a legitimate film credit
jokes.explanation: 'Hot industrial flick' is a genuinely funny euphemism that reveals Andy's self-inflation perfectly. The word 'hot' doing heavy lifting to make corporate video sound glamorous is sharp economy.

jokes.text: 'On this show, all three judges are mean.'
jokes.setup: Andy describes the show's format with enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: His one distinguishing feature of the show is that all three judges are mean — treating cruelty as the selling point
jokes.explanation: Sharp media satire in one sentence. The idea that 'all three are mean' is the show's innovation, delivered with pride by someone who should be nervous about this, is solid observational comedy about reality TV culture.

jokes.text: Dwight's confessional on his new dynamic with Jim: 'Once upon a time, we were natural enemies, but we've overcome our differences, much like Germany and Italy in World War...' Jim cuts him off: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Dwight begins an analogy about former enemies becoming allies
jokes.punchline: He reaches for WWII Axis powers — countries that allied in a war of global conquest — as his friendship metaphor, and Jim preemptively shuts it down before he finishes
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels simultaneously: Dwight's obliviousness (he thinks this is a flattering analogy) and Jim's long familiarity with Dwight's thought patterns allowing him to kill it with a single 'No' before it lands. The incomplete analogy is funnier than any punchline would be. 'Good call' from Jim adds a perfect button. Excellent structure and economy — one of the episode's strongest bits.

jokes.text: Dwight and Jim's confessional: 'Together, we run a no-nonsense office.' Cut to the office doing something clearly chaotic/goofy.
jokes.setup: Dwight solemnly declares they run a 'no-nonsense office'
jokes.punchline: The cut to the actual office (implied by the [04:56] timestamp showing Jim and Pam giggling about 'pre-conference room meeting') ironizes the claim
jokes.explanation: A mild situational irony joke that the transcript doesn't fully land — we can infer the contrast but it's not as sharp as it would be on screen. Functional but not standout.

jokes.text: Jim and Dwight's confessional pre/post-meeting ritual: 'Preconference room meeting with Dwight went really well.' / 'Oh. Bodes well for the post-conference room meeting.' / 'All depends on the conference room meeting itself.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Dwight now have a pre-meeting meeting structure they're both enthusiastic about
jokes.punchline: The recursive meeting logic — a meeting to prepare for the meeting, with the intermediate meeting being the variable — delivered with full bureaucratic seriousness
jokes.explanation: A sharp piece of office satire — the absurdity of meta-meetings is a real corporate phenomenon, and the ping-pong delivery between Jim and Dwight (two people who normally fight) makes it funnier. The logical structure of the three-meeting system is internally consistent, which elevates it above pure absurdism.

jokes.text: Dwight's inspirational quote: 'Some say the only failure there is is the failure to try. That is wrong. Failure of any kind is failure.'
jokes.setup: Dwight announces he likes to begin each meeting with an inspirational quote
jokes.punchline: His 'inspirational quote' is a direct contradiction of the quote — a demotivational statement delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The joke perfectly encapsulates Dwight's management philosophy: he frames a harshly pessimistic statement as inspiration, and the structure (quoting a real inspirational sentiment, then immediately refuting it) is beautifully efficient. Only Dwight would consider 'failure of any kind is failure' a morale-boosting opener. Strong structure, excellent character integration, highly quotable.

jokes.text: Jim's 'Michael J. Fax from fax to the future' bit — laying out hypothetical nonsense to illustrate what zero nonsense means
jokes.setup: Jim explains that the office has a 'no nonsense' policy and gives an example of what that means
jokes.punchline: 'Michael J. Fax from fax to the future' as the example of forbidden nonsense
jokes.explanation: Jim doing what Jim does best — finding the one specific, perfectly calibrated joke within a situation. 'Michael J. Fax' is a solid pun with good wordplay construction. The framing (listing what NOT to say, thereby saying it) is a classic comic structure well executed.

jokes.text: Kevin bursting in: 'Daycare won't take Phillip anymore. Why? Apparently my station in life has descended to a depth even they won't forgive.'
jokes.setup: The meeting is derailed by Angela's baby Phillip being rejected from daycare
jokes.punchline: The rejection is framed not as logistics but as a moral/social judgment on Angela's life station — she's being condemned even by daycare providers
jokes.explanation: 'My station in life has descended to a depth even they won't forgive' is a wonderfully melodramatic framing of a daycare rejection. The pomposity of the phrasing against the mundaneness of the situation is classic Office character comedy. Angela treating social embarrassment as a Greek tragedy is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: Meredith's confessional: 'I've been on my best behavior for nine years. If it wasn't for the cameras, I would've done some truly vulgar crap.'
jokes.setup: Characters react to the documentary airing tonight; Meredith reflects on nine years of documented behavior
jokes.punchline: She's been holding back this whole time — the cameras actually improved her behavior, and 'truly vulgar crap' is what she's capable of
jokes.explanation: An outstanding Meredith line that recontextualizes the entire series. The implication that nine seasons of Meredith's documented depravity was the RESTRAINED version is genuinely shocking and funny. 'Truly vulgar crap' is perfectly Meredith in its bluntness. Strong character integration — this joke literally only works for Meredith. A strong 8.

jokes.text: Oscar's confessional: 'Over the course of this documentary, I've had three affairs. If you find my body in a ditch, let me save the police some trouble. My wife did it.'
jokes.setup: Characters react to the documentary airing; Oscar reflects on what viewers are about to learn about him
jokes.punchline: He pre-emptively names his own murder suspect — his wife — in case the documentary leads to his death
jokes.explanation: Exceptional construction: the escalation from 'I've had affairs' to pre-filing a murder report is a beautiful comedic escalation, and the deadpan 'let me save the police some trouble' adds black comedy gravity. The specificity ('my wife did it') after establishing the cause-and-effect is perfectly efficient. Highly quotable and deeply dark. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Kevin confessional: 'When this thing started, I was still having sex with women. As was Kevin, I believe.' — then Oscar adding the Kevin bit
jokes.setup: Kevin reflects on how much has changed since the documentary began filming
jokes.punchline: Kevin implies he no longer has sex with women (ambiguously — through exhaustion or failure) then Oscar adds 'as was Kevin, I believe' — treating Kevin's sex life as a historical curiosity requiring scholarly qualification
jokes.explanation: The joke works in layers: Kevin's wistful nostalgia for his own heterosexuality is funny on its own, but Oscar's journalistic addendum 'as was Kevin, I believe' — as if he needs to verify Kevin's past — elevates it significantly. 'I believe' implies Oscar finds this historically dubious.

jokes.text: Kevin's announcement: 'Some of us whose televisions got broken during an all-you-can-eat shrimp commercial will be watching at Poor Richard's. But note, all are welcome, not just those who saw an all-you-can-eat shrimp commercial and charged their televisions.'
jokes.setup: Kevin announces an alternative viewing location
jokes.punchline: He accidentally reveals he broke his TV watching a shrimp commercial and charged it, then immediately tries to clarify that the REASON for his invitation isn't this embarrassing story he just told everyone
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed Kevin joke. The accidental self-exposure (breaking his TV during a shrimp commercial) is very Kevin — his greed and impulsiveness implied in a single detail. The second sentence making it worse by repeating the embarrassing detail while trying to disavow it is classic comedy.

jokes.text: Ryan confessional: 'This airs tonight? Oh my God. If my parents see this, I am toast.'
jokes.setup: Characters react to the documentary airing; Ryan contemplates parental judgment
jokes.punchline: Ryan — who has done genuinely criminal things over nine seasons — is most worried about what his parents will think
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy that relies entirely on the viewer knowing Ryan's history. 'I am toast' is a bit flat. Works as an ensemble moment but isn't especially sharp on its own.

jokes.text: Andy's Martin Luther King speech: 'Can you imagine if Martin Luther King were here and sang I Dreamed a Dream from Les Mis? With that baritone? That would be historic.'
jokes.setup: Andy is hyped up about the singing competition and makes a grandiose comparison
jokes.punchline: He imagines MLK singing a Les Misérables song at a singing competition, then focuses on the practical vocal quality ('that baritone') as the clincher for why it would be 'historic'
jokes.explanation: Weirdly specific in a funny way — the convergence of MLK, Les Mis, and a singing competition works because of Andy's enthusiasm for the detail ('that baritone'). The fact that 'historic' refers to a great singing performance rather than civil rights is the tonal collision that makes it work. Feels authentically Andy.

jokes.text: Andy and the competition host's mutual admiration exchange, culminating in 'Pour some Sugar Ray on me!'
jokes.setup: Andy bonds with the MC of the singing competition, feeling the social connection
jokes.punchline: 'Pour some Sugar Ray on me' — a mangled version of 'Pour Some Sugar on Me' (Def Leppard) with 'Sugar Ray' substituted, either from Andy's confusion between bands or as a pun on 'Sugar Ray Leonard' in a sports context
jokes.explanation: The mixed-up band reference (Def Leppard/Sugar Ray) is funny partly because Andy doesn't even clock it — he's just riding the wave of social energy. 'I don't know where it came from' is a good button. Character-specific in Andy's enthusiastic-but-sloppy way.

jokes.text: The AARM hierarchy breakdown: 'Someone to whisper in the ear of the consigliore.' / 'You've got a regional manager... a loyal but bungling apostle... but what about the assistant assistant to the regional manager?'
jokes.setup: Jim pitches Dwight on the idea of creating a new hierarchical position
jokes.punchline: The elaborate quasi-Mafia/Arthurian framing for what is, in practice, a third-tier administrative role at a paper company; the description 'loyal but bungling apostle' for the current assistant
jokes.explanation: The layered metaphors (consigliore, apostle, King Arthur) applied to a mid-level paper company position is good absurdist comedy. 'Loyal but bungling apostle' is a standout phrase. Works because both Jim and Dwight are fully committed to the gravity of the conversation.

jokes.text: Jim: 'How would King Arthur choose the next knight of his round table?' Dwight: 'That doesn't sound crazy, Jim. That's the sanest thing I've ever heard.'
jokes.setup: Jim suggests using King Arthur's methodology to select the new office position
jokes.punchline: Dwight endorses the King Arthur criterion as the SANEST thing he's ever heard — the inversion of normal sanity standards perfectly reflecting Dwight's value system
jokes.explanation: Dwight calling something 'the sanest thing I've ever heard' when it's objectively absurd is a beautifully inverted character moment. Strong character integration — the line could only land the way it does because of nine seasons establishing what Dwight considers 'sane.'

jokes.text: Andy locking in his starting note: '♪ A 440 ♪' then: 'A cappella is all about pitch, and I am nothing if not a total pitch bitch.'
jokes.setup: Andy is preparing for his audition with great seriousness
jokes.punchline: 'I am nothing if not a total pitch bitch' — a rhyming self-description that sounds like a legitimate musician's credential but is extremely crass
jokes.explanation: The rhyme and the earnest delivery make 'pitch bitch' genuinely quotable. Andy's mixture of musical precision (A 440 is technically correct) with crude braggadocio is perfectly calibrated to his character.

jokes.text: The show host accidentally revealing there's a mole, then immediately backpedaling: 'Oops. I'm not supposed to -- not supposed to say that. All right. No mole. Forget I said it.'
jokes.setup: The competition host is running through show parameters for the crowd
jokes.punchline: He accidentally reveals there's a secret mole in the competition, then awkwardly walks it back in real time
jokes.explanation: A functional reality-TV satire beat — the incompetent presenter revealing things he shouldn't is a reliable comic structure. The backpedaling dialogue is well-written but the joke type (accidental reveal) is fairly standard.

jokes.text: Dwight's announcement: 'Members of the office, hear ye. That means ye, Plop.'
jokes.setup: Dwight addresses the office with a formal proclamation
jokes.punchline: Specifically calling out Pete (nicknamed 'Plop') by the embarrassing nickname, as if 'hear ye' might not apply to him
jokes.explanation: The 'Plop' nickname running gag gets a brief deployment here. The formality of 'hear ye' + the casual cruelty of 'Plop' is the joke. Functional but minor.

jokes.text: Dwight announces the AARM position: 'You'll always have the upper hand when you've got a good AARM.' / '— Trademark pending.'
jokes.setup: Dwight introduces the new assistant position by its acronym
jokes.punchline: AARM is a pun on 'arm,' and he's already trademarked it — the level of preparation for a joke about an office job role
jokes.explanation: The 'trademark pending' detail is what elevates this beyond a simple pun — it implies Dwight spent time and potentially money preparing this wordplay for the office announcement. Good character integration.

jokes.text: 'Sure, every participant will be getting a corn dog, but that's for fueling only. No savoring.'
jokes.setup: Dwight announces the AARM competition will have corn dogs
jokes.punchline: 'No savoring' — the corn dog is a functional energy delivery system, not a pleasure device; treating enjoyment of food as a policy violation
jokes.explanation: 'No savoring' is an exceptional two-word punchline. It encapsulates Dwight's entire worldview — efficiency over pleasure, discipline over enjoyment — in the most mundane possible context (corn dog consumption). Highly quotable and deeply character-specific. Strong economy.

jokes.text: Jim's mock-envious aside about the AARM competition: 'Wow. What an honor.' / 'God, I envy them.' / 'He envies you.' / 'You don't need to repeat right now...'
jokes.setup: Jim (who is already assistant) watches others be selected for the AARM trials
jokes.punchline: Jim sarcastically envies the participants; Dwight literally repeats his envy to the group; Jim has to explain that real-time repetition undermines the bit
jokes.explanation: The meta-joke of Jim and Dwight's comedy partnership (Dwight missing the point of a bit and Jim having to explain it) is a nice evolution of their dynamic. The fact that Dwight repeats it earnestly is the strongest element.

jokes.text: Dwight's confessional: 'By 2:00, Dwight will choose himself to be assistant to his own assistant, me.'
jokes.setup: Dwight explains the AARM selection process in a confessional
jokes.punchline: He's telegraphing that he'll appoint himself — the entire elaborate selection process is theater for a conclusion already determined
jokes.explanation: Good foreshadowing joke — the viewer can laugh at knowing the elaborate competition is rigged, while also appreciating Dwight's total lack of self-awareness about broadcasting the fix. The recursive phrasing 'assistant to his own assistant, me' is nicely tangled.

jokes.text: Darryl reveals he's been secretly moving furniture: 'Delivered all my furniture to Philly.' / 'I pulled the old Irish Exit. Just slipped out without making a big deal. No hard feelings. No feelings at all.'
jokes.setup: Darryl appears to have returned; it's revealed he's been quietly moving out during what looked like normal workdays
jokes.punchline: 'No hard feelings. No feelings at all.' — the stoic correction reveals the Irish Exit was emotional avoidance as much as logistics
jokes.explanation: The self-correction from 'no hard feelings' to 'no feelings at all' is a beautifully economical bit of character writing — revealing Darryl's emotional armor in real time. The Irish Exit concept applied to a decade-long workplace relationship adds appropriate absurdity.

jokes.text: AARM Challenge 1: Dwight asks Meredith what number he's thinking of. 'Two.' / '985,000,000,000,017.' / 'Not even close, Meredith.'
jokes.setup: Dwight tests whether candidates can read his mind — asking what number he's thinking of
jokes.punchline: He was thinking of 985,000,000,000,017 — a number so specific and enormous that the challenge was always unwinnable
jokes.explanation: The number 985,000,000,000,017 is a perfect joke. It's not round, it's not a 'funny number,' it's just a massive, arbitrary, specific number — which implies Dwight had it ready, which implies this was always a gotcha. The deadpan 'not even close' is the ideal button. Excellent structure and character integration — Dwight's mind-reading test reflecting his delusion of being uniquely inscrutable.

jokes.text: Pam answers the mind-reading challenge with 'Saved by the Bell' theme — Dwight: 'It was the theme song to Boy Meets World.' Then Jim objects: 'You're trying to give your wife this job.' Dwight: 'That's exactly what I was doing.'
jokes.setup: Dwight tests Pam on mind-reading; she gets it slightly wrong (wrong TGIF show); Jim accuses Dwight of cheating for Pam
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately and shamelessly admits he was trying to give her the job — no attempt to deny it
jokes.explanation: The blatant admission of favoritism is very funny — Dwight being caught and immediately confessing with zero shame. The TGIF detail (Saved by the Bell vs. Boy Meets World) is specific and nostalgic in a way that rewards engaged viewers. Good structure.

jokes.text: Pete (Plop) answers 'a horse' — Dwight: 'Ew, the exact opposite, actually.' / 'What's the opposite of a horse?' / 'Come on. It's sea horse.' / 'A sea horse.' / Dwight: 'Whoa, how did you know that I was gonna... Say that? Uncanny.'
jokes.setup: Pete guesses 'horse' for Dwight's animal. Dwight says it's the exact opposite. Jim says the opposite of a horse is a seahorse. Dwight is astonished Jim knew his follow-up.
jokes.punchline: Dwight treating a seahorse as the objective opposite of a horse (debatable at best), and then being amazed Jim anticipated he would say that — as if it were mystical insight rather than the obvious joke
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly constructed multi-beat joke. The layers: (1) 'exact opposite' of horse being a random judgment call, (2) Jim immediately knowing what Dwight's 'opposite' would be (because Jim knows Dwight so well), (3) Dwight being genuinely astonished by Jim's insight, (4) 'Uncanny' as the button — treating their comedy partnership as magical prophecy. This is the Jim-Dwight relationship at its finest. One of the episode's top three moments.

jokes.text: Clark's AARM challenge: reading a phone message aloud including 'Yuri big nose' in front of the Turkish ambassador — 'God! Besides, the whole thing is a trick question. There's no Turkish ambassador to Armenia. The two countries don't have diplomatic relations.'
jokes.setup: Clark is tested on proper message etiquette; the scenario includes a Turkish ambassador who is 'extremely embarrassed about the size of his nose'
jokes.punchline: Clark reads the message aloud including the nose insult; Dwight's correction reveals the entire scenario was a trick (Turkey and Armenia have no diplomatic relations)
jokes.explanation: The joke has a nice double-layered construction: the obvious blunder (reading 'Yuri big nose' aloud) and then the surprise that the whole scenario was geopolitically impossible from the start. Dwight's knowledge of Turkish-Armenian diplomatic relations as an office management tool is wonderfully specific and character-defining.

jokes.text: Andy's confessional about other contestants' feel-good stories: 'Great. More screen time for the war vet. All you gotta do is risk your life for this country and everyone goes Gaga for you.'
jokes.setup: Andy discovers that contestants with compelling backstories (war vets, single mothers) are getting preferential screen time
jokes.punchline: He resents the war veteran's life sacrifice as an unfair competitive advantage in a singing show
jokes.explanation: Andy's resentment of someone for 'risking their life' as a career move is pitch-perfect character comedy — the extreme narcissism of treating military service as a PR strategy to be jealous of. Only Andy would say this earnestly. The irony lands hard because Andy has no self-awareness about how awful it sounds.

jokes.text: Andy decides to manufacture his own feel-good story: 'They want feel-good stories? Wait till they get a good feel of me.'
jokes.setup: Andy is worried about the competition's preference for feel-good backstory contestants
jokes.punchline: 'Wait till they get a good feel of me' — an unintentionally suggestive phrase delivered with complete sincerity as a motivational declaration
jokes.explanation: A solid Andy malapropism — the phrase is genuinely odd-sounding and Andy doesn't notice. Works as quick character humor.

jokes.text: Darryl's candid assessment of Jim's life choices: 'Jim is happy here, selling paper at Dunder Mifflin?' / 'That's what he says.' / 'If you say so.'
jokes.setup: Pam relays that Jim claims to be happy; Darryl has just described his own life (eating steak with sports heroes in 32 cities)
jokes.punchline: Darryl's incredulous repetition and 'if you say so' says everything — politely devastating skepticism about Jim's contentment
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is in what's NOT said. Darryl's restraint — just repeating the claim and adding 'if you say so' — is perfectly calibrated. It also carries genuine narrative weight for the Jim/Pam storyline, making it emotionally resonant comedy. The juxtaposition with Darryl's own exciting life makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Phyllis delivers the coffee directly to Dwight: 'Here's your coffee! Ow! My skin! Ow! Ow! Aah! It burns! Aah!'
jokes.setup: Phyllis finally delivers the coffees but can barely hold them due to how hot they are
jokes.punchline: She dumps burning hot coffee on herself/Dwight in dramatic fashion — 'My skin! It burns!'
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the obstacle course bit — physical comedy that plays much bigger on screen than in transcript. The 'my skin' screaming is broad slapstick; functional but not especially crafted. High impact because physical burns always get a reaction from live audiences.

jokes.text: Darryl's non-goodbye catches up with him: warehouse workers drag him upstairs; he narrates 'So, I'm going upstairs.'
jokes.setup: The warehouse crew discovers Darryl tried to Irish Exit without saying goodbye and physically forces him to come upstairs
jokes.punchline: After being manhandled upstairs by an angry mob: 'So, I'm going upstairs.' — resigned acceptance stated flatly
jokes.explanation: The deadpan understatement of a man being physically forced to a location narrating it matter-of-factly is very Darryl. Good economy — four words carry the complete resignation.

jokes.text: Jim reveals the AARM candidate: 'The only possible assistant to my assistant is... Me.' Dwight: 'The new assistant to the assistant to the regional manager is... Dwight K. Schrute.' Dwight kneels, then: 'The manager for Dunder Mifflin kneels for no man.'
jokes.setup: The AARM competition concludes; both Jim and Dwight simultaneously realize the only candidate is Dwight himself
jokes.punchline: Dwight begins to kneel, then catches himself — the manager kneels for no man — standing back up to preserve his dignity while appointing himself to a subordinate position
jokes.explanation: The joke has great structure: the elaborate competition → obvious foregone conclusion → the self-appointment → the dignity-preservation about kneeling while having just appointed himself to serve himself. The recursive logic of Dwight as both boss and subordinate is perfectly absurd and character-specific. 'The manager for Dunder Mifflin kneels for no man' is a great line.

jokes.text: Dwight asks Jim to kneel for the AARM investiture: 'I think you might want to kneel for this.' Jim: 'And yet, the manager for Dunder Mifflin kneels for no man.'
jokes.setup: Dwight wants Jim to kneel for the ceremonial moment of becoming AARM
jokes.punchline: Jim responds with mock-regal gravitas — 'the manager for Dunder Mifflin kneels for no man' — a perfectly calibrated straight-man response
jokes.explanation: A nice riff on medieval ceremony applied to a paper company. Jim's dignified refusal, delivered in suitably mock-heroic language, is a great deadpan beat. The absurdity of the situation elevates the line.

jokes.text: Dwight's new policy: 'From now on, anyone who needs to speak to me has got to go through me first, all right?'
jokes.setup: Dwight announces the new chain of command following his AARM appointment
jokes.punchline: The policy requires going through Dwight to reach Dwight — a bureaucratic impossibility stated as a logical directive
jokes.explanation: A brilliant line that ranks among the episode's best. The self-referential paradox (you must go through Dwight to get to Dwight) is stated with complete seriousness as a workable management policy. Maximum funny per word — one sentence encapsulates the entire AARM absurdity. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific. Approaches calibration anchor territory.

jokes.text: The office employees mob Darryl with requests for his final hours: one-on-one lunch at Cugino's, van time listening to Zeppelin, recording his stories for '6 or 8 or 10 hours.' Kevin wants to watch an eHow video on Excel before scheduling Darryl's 12 hours in 90-minute segments.
jokes.setup: The office workers realize Darryl is leaving and they've never properly spent time with him
jokes.punchline: The requests escalate from reasonable (lunch) to absurd (6-10 hours of recorded stories) to Kevin's plan to watch an Excel tutorial FIRST before beginning the scheduling
jokes.explanation: A good ensemble escalation. Kevin's aside about needing to watch an eHow Excel video first is the standout beat — his priorities completely wrong-headed but very Kevin. The 90-minute segment plan is also a good detail.

jokes.text: Creed: 'Darryl, you know, I would love to just record some of your stories, just let the tape roll for six or eight or ten hours, and just see what we get.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is competing to claim time with departing Darryl
jokes.punchline: Creed's version of quality time is a six-to-ten-hour unstructured confession session — implying Creed has done something like this before and knows the value of 'just seeing what we get' from unguarded marathon interviews
jokes.explanation: Creed's idea of a farewell is a forensic interrogation session — 'just see what we get' implies fishing for incriminating material or strange confession. The range ('six or eight or ten hours') being this specific and large is very Creed. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Kevin using his pen as a fidget toy during a confessional, explaining defensively: 'I'm moving the ink down in my pen, for work.' / 'Here, use my pen.' / 'Don't tell me what to do!'
jokes.setup: Kevin is clicking/moving his pen annoyingly; Angela offers hers
jokes.punchline: Kevin's volcanic 'Don't tell me what to do!' in response to a simple pen offer — the disproportionate anger to an innocent gesture
jokes.explanation: 'For work' as a justification for the pen-fidgeting is a good Kevin absurdism — trying to legitimize a mindless habit as purposeful. The disproportionate anger at Angela is very Kevin. Solid character comedy.

jokes.text: Kevin storming off: 'And you obviously don't need me. / Kevin, where are you going? / Away. / Tell Phillip that his stupid little baby wish came true.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is upset and leaving in a huff
jokes.punchline: 'Tell Phillip that his stupid little baby wish came true' — Kevin believes the infant made a wish that resulted in his dismissal, and wants the baby to know it worked
jokes.explanation: An outstanding Kevin line. The premise — that an infant made a deliberate wish and Kevin is consciously acknowledging it came true — reveals Kevin's complete inability to distinguish baby behavior from adult intention. 'His stupid little baby wish' is perfectly specific. The wounded dignity in informing the baby of its victory is hilarious. One of the episode's most quotable moments and a strong case for a top-3 finish.

jokes.text: Dwight and Angela discussing Phillip eating paper: 'Earlier today he tried to eat some of the 24-weight letter bond.' / 'Smart baby. That's the most flavorful bond.'
jokes.setup: Phillip is captivated by office paper; Angela mentions he tried to eat some
jokes.punchline: Dwight endorses eating 24-weight letter bond specifically as the 'most flavorful' — speaking from experience
jokes.explanation: The implication that Dwight has personal opinions on the flavor of different paper weights — formed through tasting them — is perfectly surreal and deeply character-specific. 'That's the most flavorful bond' suggests not just that he's eaten paper, but that he has a refined palate about it. Excellent character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Andy in disguise as 'Ezra Cornell': 'No, no, I'm wearing makeup. / You did a really great job. / You even look shorter. / Oh, I took out my lifts. / Yeah, unlike Andy Bernard, this character is my real height.'
jokes.setup: Andy has returned in disguise as an old man named Ezra Cornell to get another audition shot
jokes.punchline: The disguise confirmation reveals Andy normally wears height-enhancing lifts in his shoes — his real height is shorter than his performance height
jokes.explanation: The lift revelation is a perfect detail — Andy's vanity and self-image issues expressed through shoe inserts. 'Unlike Andy Bernard, this character is my real height' is a great line that collapses the disguise-within-disguise concept neatly.

jokes.text: Dwight's confession of his life on the farm: 'All day long, it's moo the cows and cluck the hens. Get the sheep baa-ed. Oink the pigs. Oink the pigs, that is very important.'
jokes.setup: Esther is describing the farm work to Dwight
jokes.punchline: 'Oink the pigs, that is very important' — the escalating list of animal noise responsibilities, with pigs specifically called out as critical
jokes.explanation: The running list of farm tasks is moderately funny, but 'oink the pigs, that is very important' is the standout beat — the singling out of pig-oinking as particularly crucial is a good absurdist touch.

jokes.text: Dwight spacing out while Angela talks about farm animals, then snapping back: 'Dwight? / The way that boy looks at the Galactica is precisely the way I look at the Galactica. And he eats the same kind of paper I do.'
jokes.setup: Angela lists farm animal duties while Dwight is mentally elsewhere; the camera (implied) catches Dwight staring at Phillip
jokes.punchline: Dwight's internal monologue reveals he's bonding with the baby over their shared interest in the Battlestar Galactica model and mutual paper-eating habits
jokes.explanation: The callback to the paper-eating moment elevated by adding the Galactica detail — Dwight diagnosing paternity through shared nerd interests. 'He eats the same kind of paper I do' as a bonding criterion is a perfect expression of Dwight's alien value system. Strong character integration — this joke literally could not belong to any other character.

jokes.text: Dwight introduces his 'number two' to help with the baby test: 'He's the best in the biz. Unless you think he can't handle it.' / 'Hey, he can handle it.'
jokes.setup: Dwight needs someone to administer a paternity test on the baby
jokes.punchline: He delegates to his 'best in the biz' number two — who is himself — creating a moment where he has to vouch for himself as if in third person
jokes.explanation: A nice payoff to the AARM structure — Dwight being his own number two has a practical consequence where he must defend his own competence to a skeptic. The recursive self-advocacy is funny.

jokes.text: Dwight warns Phillip about waking the 'grumpy old walrus' — Stanley: 'I heard that.' / Mama.
jokes.setup: Dwight is trying to quiet the baby near the sleeping Stanley
jokes.punchline: Stanley, described as a 'grumpy old walrus,' immediately responds 'I heard that' — proving he was awake/partially awake; then the baby says 'Mama' as a non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: The 'grumpy old walrus' is a good Dwight insult (specific animal, not just 'grumpy'), and Stanley's immediate 'I heard that' is a classic reaction beat. The baby's 'Mama' as a punctuation mark is an unscripted-feeling button.

jokes.text: Mose's credentials for baby care: 'Pam can attest, there's no one better at getting brats to shut their yaps.' Pam: 'He does have a gift.'
jokes.setup: Mose volunteers to take the baby; claims expertise
jokes.punchline: His baby-care credential is 'getting brats to shut their yaps' — parenting as noise suppression. Pam endorses this.
jokes.explanation: Mose's child-management philosophy ('shut their yaps') contrasted with Pam's earnest endorsement ('he does have a gift') is a solid double-act beat. The formulation treats silence as the singular metric of successful childcare.

jokes.text: Baby Phillip chooses the beet; Dwight: 'Yeah. / Any ordinary child would have taken the money, but you're no ordinary child, are you? No. I can tell by your gorgeous, widely-set eyes.'
jokes.setup: Phillip has chosen the beet, confirming Schrute DNA in Dwight's assessment
jokes.punchline: Dwight adds a physical confirmation — the 'widely-set eyes' as a Schrute family trait, reading a baby's face like a livestock judge examining bloodlines
jokes.explanation: A good button on the beet scene — Dwight's physical assessment of the baby ('widely-set eyes') as a Schrute trait adds another dimension to the absurdism. Treating infant facial structure as bloodline evidence is both funny and surprisingly tender.

jokes.text: Andy's physical altercation with the bouncer, screaming 'I'm Casey Dean! You'll be seeing the last of me! Or — I meant you won't be seeing the last of me!'
jokes.setup: Andy is being physically removed from the audition
jokes.punchline: In his moment of defiant exit, he botches his own threat — 'you'll be seeing the last of me' means the opposite of what he intends, and he immediately corrects himself, destroying any dramatic impact
jokes.explanation: The botched threat is Andy's tragedy in miniature — he can't even execute a defiant exit properly. 'I'm Casey Dean!' shouted in his alter ego while being physically removed, followed by an immediate self-correction, is genuinely funny and sad. The self-correction ruins his own moment and he can't stop himself.

jokes.text: He just keeps spitting out the nipple. / That's because this baby is of superior intelligence. He can tell when he's being tricked out of the experience of a real human breast. / He's not that smart. He doesn't know where I hid his duck.
jokes.setup: Pam says Phillip won't take a bottle
jokes.punchline: Dwight diagnoses it as Schrute superior intelligence; Pam deflates this with 'he doesn't know where I hid his duck' — a perfectly calibrated proof of ordinary baby cognition
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure. Dwight's confident diagnosis of baby superiority is immediately punctured by Pam's specific, mundane evidence: 'he doesn't know where I hid his duck.' The specificity of the hidden duck as the counter-argument is perfect — it's not a grand rebuttal, just one small, very real baby fact. One of the episode's best exchanges.

jokes.text: Show judge seeing through Andy's 'Ezra Cornell' disguise immediately: 'No, you're a middle-aged man with a lot of makeup on.'
jokes.setup: Andy presents himself as 'Ezra Cornell, kindly old fellow with a song in my heart'
jokes.punchline: The judge flatly and immediately sees through it with clinical accuracy
jokes.explanation: The economy is excellent — 'a middle-aged man with a lot of makeup on' is perfectly unvarnished. The joke works because of the complete deflation of Andy's elaborate setup, but the punchline itself isn't especially inventive.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Busted. Got it. Yes, all right. Tried to get your attention with tricks, but you just want to hear me sing. I respect that.' / Judge: 'We do not want to hear you sing.'
jokes.setup: Andy graciously accepts the unmasking and reframes it as mutual respect for authenticity
jokes.punchline: The judge immediately corrects him — they don't want to hear him sing either
jokes.explanation: Andy's confident misreading of the situation ('you just want to hear me sing') followed by the immediate correction is a good misdirection structure. Andy's optimism as a defense mechanism is well-deployed here.

jokes.text: Andy's bid for sympathy: 'Slept in my car last night. Quit my job, burned all my bridges. I went to the bathroom on my boss's car. And I did unspeakable things with Carla Fern.' / Judge: 'Ugh, flag on the play.'
jokes.setup: Andy tries to manufacture a feel-good backstory to earn sympathy from the judges
jokes.punchline: The escalating confessions reach 'unspeakable things with Carla Fern' — a mystery name that implies something too awful to specify; 'flag on the play' as sports-referee language applied to casual conversation
jokes.explanation: The escalation is well-structured: each new revelation is worse than the last, and 'unspeakable things with Carla Fern' is perfect because it implies everything without specifying anything. 'Flag on the play' is a great reaction that uses sports language as a social objection tool. Good structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Andy sings the Cornell fight song 'Far Above Cayuga's Waters' to the judges. Judge: 'What is this song?' Andy: 'Are you insane? It's the Cornell fight song.'
jokes.setup: Andy, desperate to stay in the audition, chooses a song to sing
jokes.punchline: His song choice is his college fight song — a wildly inappropriate audition song that he defends with complete incredulity
jokes.explanation: Andy's Cornell pride driving him to sing the fight song in a crisis is perfectly on-character — his identity has always been wrapped up in his Ivy League status. 'Are you insane? It's the Cornell fight song' delivered with genuine offense is a great Andy beat.

jokes.text: Judge to Andy after his Cornell fight song: 'Look, man, you're not terrible but we've heard a lot of really good singers today, and you're just not good enough.' Andy: 'Wow, you guys are really mean.' / 'I guess that's the show.'
jokes.setup: Andy protests that he's being judged unfairly after they let him sing
jokes.punchline: Andy discovers that 'all judges are mean' is a personal experience, not just a show format description — then immediately reconnects it to the show's premise as if it explains everything
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'all three judges are mean' lands because Andy identified this as the show's feature without anticipating it would apply to him. 'I guess that's the show' is a resigned acknowledgment. Solid callback structure.

jokes.text: Andy crying in the judge's chair: 'You can't just sit here and cry.' / 'Oh, I can so just sit here and cry!'
jokes.setup: Andy is devastated by rejection and collapses emotionally in the judges' area
jokes.punchline: The defiant 'I can so just sit here and cry!' — asserting the right to public emotional breakdown with full commitment
jokes.explanation: Andy's emotional incontinence is a well-established character trait, and this is a strong expression of it. The defiance in asserting his right to cry makes it funnier than simple weeping. Highly quotable — the specific construction 'I can SO just sit here and cry' captures Andy's wounded dignity.

jokes.text: Kevin: 'Can't hear you. I'm giving you the silence treatment.' / 'How does it feel being ignored?'
jokes.setup: Kevin is giving someone the silent treatment but immediately breaks it to explain he's doing so
jokes.punchline: 'Silence treatment' (instead of 'silent treatment') + asking how it feels to be ignored while actively engaging — destroying the silent treatment by executing it
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent Kevin joke. The malapropism ('silence treatment') is classic Kevin, but the structural comedy — immediately breaking the silent treatment to ask how it feels — is a perfect logical contradiction that only Kevin would commit. The self-undermining nature of the joke is beautifully constructed. Strong across all metrics. One of the episode's best standalone jokes.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'That was a really cool move.' (about Phillip buying Kevin a gift card) / Kevin holding Phillip: 'What a chubbers. / I'm losing my balance. Whoa.'
jokes.setup: Kevin reconciles with Phillip via a $25 iTunes gift card; Kevin then holds the baby
jokes.punchline: Kevin can barely hold the baby without losing his balance — a large man destabilized by an infant
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that plays better visually. 'What a chubbers' is a funny Kevin-ism but the balance joke is relatively generic. Functional but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: Kevin's assessment of friendship with Phillip: 'He's a little standoffish at first. But once he starts buying you things, man, you can tell he likes you.'
jokes.setup: Kevin reflects on his new relationship with Phillip the baby
jokes.punchline: Kevin's theory of friendship is entirely transactional — gift-giving is how you know someone likes you, applied earnestly to a baby who can't actually make purchasing decisions
jokes.explanation: Kevin applying adult transactional friendship logic to an infant is excellent character comedy. His genuine belief that the baby chose and purchased that gift card reveals Kevin's world model — and it's a touching version of Kevin stupidity that has warmth. 'Once he starts buying you things' is very quotable.

jokes.text: We want to dance with you. / You want to dance? / One dance. All of us together.
jokes.setup: Darryl is asked what one thing he'll do before leaving
jokes.punchline: The office's one wish is a group dance — surprisingly earnest and sweet, which makes it funny through sincerity
jokes.explanation: The joke is the sincerity. The office's collective wish being a dance feels right and funny simultaneously — it's absurd in its simplicity. Sets up the extended Boogie Wonderland sequence.

jokes.text: Dwight's marriage proposal to Angela — the business pitch format: 'She's young, she's beautiful. Genes so pure you could lick them.' / 'Her family admires me. My family tolerates hers. A lot of them are the same people because we're third cousins, which is great for bloodlines, and isn't technically incest.'
jokes.setup: Dwight lists Angela's qualities to Jim as if pitching a business investment
jokes.punchline: The pros include: genetic purity measurable by licking, families being third cousins ('not technically incest'), and a walk-in freezer of frozen cattle sperm as dowry
jokes.explanation: 'Genes so pure you could lick them' is an extraordinary phrase — the specificity of licking as a purity-testing method is surreal and perfectly Dwight. 'Isn't technically incest' as a selling point requires Dwight's exact ethical framework. The walk-in freezer of frozen cattle sperm as dowry is the escalating climax. This is an extended joke with multiple peak moments.

jokes.text: Dwight continues his pitch to Angela: '...the two of you would move to my 1,600-acre estate, which, let's face it, is a big step up from living in a gay man's closet.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is making his marriage pitch to Angela, listing the benefits of the farm
jokes.punchline: He deploys 'living in a gay man's closet' as his competitive differentiator — a callback to Oscar's joke from earlier and Dwight's characteristically blunt framing
jokes.explanation: Dwight's lack of filter applied to Angela's current living situation is good. The callback to Oscar's joke — now from Dwight's unsentimental perspective rather than Oscar's wry wordplay — is a solid but less elegant use of the same material.

jokes.text: She weaves. Colorful, durable blankets and rugs. It all adds up. / So what is the problem? / Angela.
jokes.setup: Dwight lists Esther's qualities (including weaving) as pros for the marriage
jokes.punchline: Jim asks 'so what is the problem?' and Dwight simply says 'Angela' — a one-word answer that reframes the entire pro-list as rationalization
jokes.explanation: The punchline 'Angela' — delivered as a single word after an elaborate spreadsheet of Esther's virtues — is perfectly structured comedy. The whole pro-list collapses into one word. Jim's 'so what is the problem?' sets it up perfectly and Dwight's one-word answer is the most economical punchline possible. Character integration is near-perfect — this is nine seasons of history in one word.

jokes.text: Dwight's love advice exchange with Jim: 'Every instinct, every rational calculation.' Jim: 'Some sort of virus?' / 'Love.' / 'Oh.'
jokes.setup: Jim is giving Dwight a heartfelt speech about following love over logic
jokes.punchline: As Jim builds to the word 'love,' Dwight genuinely guesses 'some sort of virus?' — suggesting his mental model for something that overrides rational thought is disease
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best-structured jokes. Jim builds a romantic speech and pauses for effect — the audience expects 'love' — but Dwight's interruption with 'some sort of virus?' reframes the entire setup. It's character-perfect (Dwight treating infection as a more rational explanation than emotion) and structurally elegant. The callback to biology as Dwight's frame for irrational behavior is very economical. Jim's 'Oh.' after finally saying 'love' is a great button.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'You're a good assistant, Jim.' / Jim: 'Not as good as you.' / Dwight: 'That's very true.' / 'Get the hell out of here.' / 'You got it.'
jokes.setup: Dwight and Jim have an emotional moment after the love confession scene
jokes.punchline: Dwight accepts Jim's compliment ('not as good as you') as pure fact with zero modesty — 'That's very true' — then dismisses him affectionately
jokes.explanation: The emotional warmth of the scene is undercut perfectly by Dwight's unironic 'That's very true' — he's incapable of false modesty even in a tender moment. The affectionate 'get the hell out of here' as a term of endearment is very Dwight. Good economy, strong character integration.

jokes.text: Darryl's confessional about his goodbye dance: 'I wanted to leave quietly. It seemed dignified. But having Kevin grind up on my front while Erin pretends to hump me from behind is a more accurate tribute to my years here.'
jokes.setup: Darryl has just danced with the whole office to 'Boogie Wonderland'
jokes.punchline: His assessment that being sandwich-grinded by coworkers is 'a more accurate tribute' to his years at Dunder Mifflin than dignified silence
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed confessional that works as genuine character insight AND as a great joke. The specificity of 'Kevin grind up on my front while Erin pretends to hump me from behind' is vivid and funny, but the philosophical acceptance — 'a more accurate tribute to my years here' — elevates it to something genuinely touching and funny simultaneously. Economy, character integration, and structure are all strong. One of the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: Oscar's goodbye to Angela: 'She doesn't know I'm living with a straight woman. I don't want to get her hopes up.'
jokes.setup: Oscar explains why he doesn't want his mother to see him dropping off Angela
jokes.punchline: His mother has apparently held out hope that Oscar will end up with a woman; Angela is not an option because she's straight — and Oscar doesn't want to raise hopes about a relationship that's categorically impossible
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — 'I don't want to get her hopes up' lands the punchline with maximum efficiency. The joke reverses the expected framing (usually about not outing yourself to family) to a scenario where the wrongness is about the woman being straight. Strong character integration and a very quotable button.

jokes.text: Dwight's roadside proposal: 'Shut up, woman! / Listen to me! I love you! And I don't care that Phillip's not my son! I will raise 100 children with 100 of your lovers if it means I can be with you!'
jokes.setup: Dwight has pulled over Angela's car to make a surprise romantic declaration
jokes.punchline: 'I will raise 100 children with 100 of your lovers' — an offer of dedication so extreme it becomes absurd; the logic of it (quantity commitment as proof of love) is uniquely Dwight
jokes.explanation: An all-time Dwight romantic declaration. The escalation from 'I love you' to 'I will raise 100 children with 100 of your lovers' is unexpected, specific, and deeply absurd. The mathematical precision (100 children, 100 lovers) as a proof of devotion is perfectly Dwight's way of expressing love — through scale and commitment metrics rather than emotion. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'This expresses how loudly I love you!' / Angela: 'It's too loud.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is blowing a loud horn (or similar instrument) to express his love's volume
jokes.punchline: Angela's flat 'It's too loud' — accepting the metaphor but requesting volume adjustment
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — two sentences, complete joke. Angela's 'it's too loud' plays the metaphor completely straight, as if she's giving feedback on audio levels rather than emotional expression. The deadpan acceptance of the conceit without challenging it is funnier than any objection would be. Both characters need to be exactly who they are for this to work.

jokes.text: Dwight's ring reintroduction: 'This is a ring taken from the buttocks of my grandmother, put there by the Gangster Patriarch of the Coors Dynasty, melted in a foundry run by Mennonites.'
jokes.setup: Dwight presents the engagement ring to Angela in his roadside proposal
jokes.punchline: The buttock-bullet ring gets a full formal reintroduction with new details — 'Gangster Patriarch of the Coors Dynasty' and 'foundry run by Mennonites' — escalating the mythology of the ring
jokes.explanation: The callback to the buttock bullet ring is magnificent. The new details ('Gangster Patriarch of the Coors Dynasty,' 'foundry run by Mennonites') expand the ring's mythology while remaining consistent with the original absurdism. The phrase 'Gangster Patriarch of the Coors Dynasty' is exceptional — it elevates Adolph Coors from named villain to dynasty patriarch. The episodic structure of the joke (introduced, used in proposal) rewards attentive viewers. This is the episode's strongest single joke moment, approaching 9+ calibration territory.

jokes.text: Angela's reveal: 'And I lied to you. / What? / Phillip's your son.' / Dwight: 'What? Why would you say that--' / 'I just needed you to want to marry me because you wanted to marry me.' / 'Get out!'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just proposed saying he doesn't care if Phillip isn't his son; Angela immediately reveals he IS the father
jokes.punchline: Angela admits she lied about paternity to test if Dwight would propose anyway — then Dwight's explosive 'Get out!' after accepting this twist
jokes.explanation: The double-reversal (paternity revealed to be true after the emotional acceptance of its untruth) is a satisfying narrative structure that also functions as dark comedy — Angela's manipulation being revealed immediately after the emotional climax. Dwight's 'Get out!' before immediately celebrating 'I'm a dad!' is perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'I'm a dad! You're a dad!' — screamed at Angela after the paternity reveal
jokes.setup: Dwight processes the news that he is actually Phillip's father
jokes.punchline: His celebration shouts 'I'm a dad! You're a dad!' — incorrectly gendering Angela in his excitement
jokes.explanation: The misdirect of 'You're a dad!' addressed to the mother in a moment of pure chaotic joy is a perfect Dwight flourish. The incorrectness isn't stupidity — it's overexcitement short-circuiting normal language. Perfect economy, highly quotable, and deeply in character.

jokes.text: Bar scene: Andy trying to get the TV changed to PBS; bartender calls a vote; tie means 'I do nothing'; Andy pleads: 'This show is about me and my attempts to find love in all the wrong places.'
jokes.setup: Andy wants the bar to change the channel to watch the documentary he's in
jokes.punchline: Andy describes the documentary as 'about me and my attempts to find love in all the wrong places' — a hilariously self-centered and slightly inaccurate description of a nine-year workplace documentary
jokes.explanation: Andy centering himself in a nine-year workplace documentary about many people is excellent character comedy. 'Attempts to find love in all the wrong places' as a description of his Dunder Mifflin arc is accidentally accurate in the funniest way. The bartender's tie-vote neutrality ('a tie means I do nothing') is also a good bit.

jokes.text: Andy's reaction to being asked how the singing audition went: 'Oh. Eh, whatever. No big deal.' (Delivered after an entire episode of epic, humiliating failure at said audition.)
jokes.setup: The whole Andy audition subplot has been a disaster
jokes.punchline: His 30-second brushoff — 'Eh, whatever. No big deal' — is the understatement of the century given what we witnessed
jokes.explanation: A good button on the Andy subplot. The gap between what we witnessed (disguise, crying, humiliation, rejection) and 'Eh, whatever. No big deal' is the whole joke. Economy is perfect. Andy's self-protective detachment is consistent with his character.

jokes.text: The documentary premiere clip shown: 'All right, Jim, your quarterlies look very good. How are things going at the library?' / 'Oh, I told you. I couldn't close it, so--' / 'So, you've come to the master for guidance? Is this what you're saying, grasshopper?' / 'Uh, actually, you called me in here.'
jokes.setup: The documentary begins airing; the first clip shown is from the series premiere — Michael claiming guru status over Jim
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'grasshopper' self-aggrandizement is immediately deflated by Jim pointing out Michael called HIM — the power dynamic was invented
jokes.explanation: The return of Michael Scott (even just in archival footage) is a major moment for the series finale run. The clip is perfectly chosen — capturing Michael's delusional authority and Jim's bemused deflation in a few lines. The impact score reflects audience reaction to Michael's return rather than pure craft, but the clip's selection is itself a craft choice. The emotional weight of this moment for long-term viewers makes it one of the episode's highest-impact beats.

tmdb_overview: Jim convinces Dwight that he needs to choose someone to act as an Assistant to the Assistant Regional Manager; the two subsequently hold tryouts for the position. After her daycare turns away her child, Angela is forced to bring her kid to work. Andy auditions for "The Next Great A Cappella Sensation".
